cell_structure_interactions_medi2200.htm.title: MEDI2200 W2 · Cell Structure & Interactions
cell_structure_interactions_medi2200.htm.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
cell_structure_interactions_medi2200.htm.content: Cytoskeleton: actin microfilaments (7-9 nm, cell-surface shape and movement), microtubules (25 nm hollow tubulin tubes, organelle positioning and transport tracks), intermediate filaments (~10 nm, mechanical strength). Actin monomer carries ATP; filament is a polar double helix with plus/barbed and minus/pointed ends; nucleation via a trimer; arrays include lamellipodium, filopodium, cortex, stress fibre. Microtubules use GTP; dynamic instability via a GTP cap; nucleated at the MTOC/centrosome with minus ends anchored. Intermediate filaments are non-polar antiparallel tetramers, no nucleotide, no motors. Motors: myosin walks actin to the plus end; kinesin walks microtubules to the plus end (anterograde), dynein to the minus end (retrograde). Cell division: actin disassembles, microtubules form the spindle, actin contractile ring in cytokinesis. Cilia/flagella: 9+2 axoneme bent by dynein arms; primary ciliary dyskinesia/Kartagener. ECM: GAGs are negatively charged and draw in water to resist compression; proteoglycans (aggrecan); collagen triple helix (Gly-X-Y) for tensile strength, types I/II/III/IV/VII; elastin for recoil; fibronectin glues matrix to cells via integrins; MMPs remodel; basal lamina = laminin + type IV collagen. Junctions apical to basal: tight (claudin/occludin seal), adherens (actin), desmosome (keratin), gap (connexons, ~1.4 nm pore), cell-matrix (integrin focal adhesion to actin; hemidesmosome to keratin). Cadherins = cell-cell; integrins = cell-matrix; anoikis = death on losing matrix anchorage.

questions.question: A tissue consists of:
options: A. A single cell and its organelles
B. Extracellular matrix with no cells
C. Cells plus the extracellular matrix between them
D. Cells packed together with no matrix
questions.explanation: A tissue = cells plus the extracellular matrix (ECM) between them, held in a shape.

questions.question: Which protein physically links the ECM outside a cell to the actin cytoskeleton inside?
questions.explanation: Integrins span the membrane, joining external matrix to internal actin; cadherins/connexins/claudins act at cell–cell junctions.

questions.question: Cancer metastasis is described as the simultaneous failure of:
options: C. The cytoskeleton, ECM and junction systems together
questions.explanation: Metastasis needs all three systems to fail at once — crawl (cytoskeleton), digest matrix, loosen junctions and re-grip.

questions.question: Which set correctly lists the three cytoskeletal filaments by diameter?
options: A. Actin 25 nm, intermediate ~10 nm, microtubules 7–9 nm
B. Actin 7–9 nm, intermediate ~10 nm, microtubules 25 nm
C. All three are about 15 nm
D. Actin ~10 nm, intermediate 25 nm, microtubules 7–9 nm
questions.explanation: Actin microfilaments (7–9 nm) are thinnest, intermediate filaments ~10 nm, microtubules (25 nm) thickest.

questions.question: Which filament chiefly provides mechanical (tensile) strength?
questions.explanation: Intermediate filaments resist tension; actin shapes the surface/moves the cell; microtubules position organelles and act as tracks.

questions.question: Microtubules mainly function to:
options: B. Position organelles and serve as transport tracks
questions.explanation: Microtubules position organelles and act as transport tracks for motor proteins.

questions.question: Building the cytoskeleton from small diffusible subunits allows it to:
options: A. Store energy for the cell
C. Be rapidly disassembled and reassembled elsewhere
questions.explanation: Small, rapidly diffusing subunits let filaments be torn down and rebuilt for division, crawling or repair.

questions.question: Which cytoskeletal filaments are polar (have distinct ends)?
questions.explanation: Actin and microtubules are polar; intermediate filaments are non-polar.

questions.question: The globular actin monomer (G-actin) carries a bound:
options: A. GTP that becomes GDP inside the filament
B. ATP that becomes ADP inside the filament
questions.explanation: G-actin binds ATP, hydrolysed to ADP once incorporated into the filament (microtubules use GTP).

questions.question: The fast-growing end of an actin filament is the:
options: C. The minus, or pointed, end
D. The plus, or barbed, end
questions.explanation: Actin grows fastest at the plus/barbed end; the minus/pointed end grows slowly.

questions.question: What determines which actin array (e.g. stress fibre vs branched lamellipodium) forms?
options: A. The concentration of ATP alone
B. The number of microtubules present
C. The nucleation protein that initiates it
questions.explanation: Different actin-binding/nucleation proteins organise actin into contractile bundles, cortex, dendritic lamellipodia or filopodia.

questions.question: Actin 'treadmilling' lets the filament:
options: A. Anchor DNA to the nuclear lamina
B. Store ATP for later use
C. Push a membrane forward by directional turnover
questions.explanation: Directional turnover (addition at the plus end, loss at the minus end) pushes membranes forward during movement.

questions.question: Microtubules are hollow tubes built from:
questions.explanation: Microtubules are 25 nm hollow tubes of alpha–beta tubulin dimers, stiffer than actin.

questions.question: Which nucleotide governs microtubule growth and shrinkage?
questions.explanation: GTP-tubulin adds at the plus end; buried GTP is hydrolysed to GDP, which favours disassembly.

questions.question: 'Dynamic instability' of a microtubule is:
options: A. Rapid switching between growing and shrinking states
B. Steady growth at a constant rate
D. Bending driven by dynein arms
questions.explanation: Dynamic instability is stochastic switching between growth (with a GTP cap) and shrinkage (cap lost).

questions.question: Microtubule minus ends are usually anchored at the:
questions.explanation: Microtubules are nucleated at the MTOC/centrosome, with minus ends anchored there and plus ends outward (except in dendrites).

questions.question: Intermediate filaments are non-polar because their tetramers are:
options: A. Antiparallel and staggered, cancelling directionality
B. Built around a GTP cap
C. All aligned in the same direction
questions.explanation: Two coiled-coil dimers form a staggered antiparallel tetramer, so the filament has no plus/minus end.

questions.question: Motor proteins do NOT run along intermediate filaments because they:
options: A. Are too thick for motors to grip
B. Have no polarity and no bound nucleotide
C. Carry a GTP cap that blocks motors
D. Are found only in the nucleus
questions.explanation: IFs lack polarity and nucleotide, so no motor proteins move on them; they are specialised for tensile strength.

questions.question: Which intermediate filaments form the nuclear lamina?
questions.explanation: Nuclear lamins A/B/C form the lamina; keratins are epithelial, vimentin mesenchymal, neurofilaments axonal.

questions.question: Mutations in which intermediate filament cause progeria?
questions.explanation: Lamin mutations cause progeria; keratin mutations cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

questions.question: Motor proteins generate movement by:
options: A. Walking along polar filaments using ATP
B. Diffusing passively through the cytosol
D. Pumping ions across the membrane
questions.explanation: Motor proteins bind polar filaments and walk along them using ATP, carrying cargo or generating force.

questions.question: Myosin walks toward the ___ end of an actin filament:
options: B. The plus, or barbed, end
C. The minus, or pointed, end
questions.explanation: Myosin moves toward the actin plus/barbed end.

questions.question: Which myosin class drives muscle contraction?
questions.explanation: Myosin II drives muscle contraction; class I acts at membranes/endocytosis; V transports organelles.

questions.question: Along a microtubule, kinesin and dynein move, respectively, toward the:
options: A. Both toward the plus end
B. The minus end, then the plus end
C. The plus end, then the minus end
D. Both toward the minus end
questions.explanation: Kinesin walks to the plus end (anterograde); dynein walks to the minus end (retrograde), aided by dynactin.

questions.question: In a neuron, transport back to the cell body (retrograde) is carried out by:
questions.explanation: Dynein is retrograde (back to the soma); kinesin is anterograde (down the axon).

questions.question: During cytokinesis, the structure that pinches the cell in two is the:
options: C. The mitotic spindle of microtubules
questions.explanation: Microtubules form the spindle; an actin–myosin II contractile ring pinches the cell in two.

questions.question: In the cell-migration cycle, the leading edge advances by extending a:
options: A. Desmosome that seals to neighbours
D. Lamellipodium that then adheres via focal adhesions
questions.explanation: Migration: extend a lamellipodium, adhere at focal adhesions, contract stress fibres to pull forward, de-adhere at the rear.

questions.question: The axoneme of a cilium or flagellum has the arrangement:
options: B. 2+9 — two doublets around nine singlets
C. 9+2 — nine outer doublets around a central pair
D. A solid bundle of microtubules
questions.explanation: The axoneme is 9+2: nine outer doublet microtubules plus a central pair, bent by dynein arms.

questions.question: Which motor protein bends the axoneme to produce ciliary movement?
questions.explanation: Dynein arms slide adjacent doublets, bending the axoneme; cilia sweep mucus and flagella propel sperm.

questions.question: The extracellular matrix is made and organised by:
questions.explanation: Cells locally secrete and organise their ECM; its proportion varies (cartilage matrix-rich, brain matrix-poor).

questions.question: Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) resist compression because they are:
options: B. Highly negatively charged, drawing in Na+ and water
questions.explanation: GAGs are unbranched, highly negative and hydrophilic; their fixed charge pulls in Na+ and water osmotically to resist compression.

questions.question: Which GAG is unsulfated and has no core protein?
questions.explanation: Hyaluronan is the only unsulfated GAG with no protein core; the others are sulfated proteoglycan GAGs.

questions.question: Aggrecan is:
options: B. A GAG with no protein core
C. A large cartilage proteoglycan that aggregates on hyaluronan
questions.explanation: Aggrecan (>100 GAG chains) aggregates on a hyaluronan backbone, giving cartilage its turgor.

questions.question: Collagen's main mechanical role is to provide:
questions.explanation: Collagen (the most abundant mammalian protein, ~25%) gives tensile strength via its triple helix and fibrils.

questions.question: Every third residue of collagen must be glycine because glycine:
options: A. It carries a strong negative charge
B. It is small enough for the crowded helix centre
C. It is the largest amino-acid residue
D. It readily forms stabilising disulfide bonds
questions.explanation: Collagen's Gly-X-Y repeat places glycine (the smallest residue) at the centre of the tight triple helix.

questions.question: Which collagen forms the basal lamina, and in what form?
options: A. Type IV, as a network/mesh
B. Type I, as thick fibres
C. Type II, as cartilage fibrils
D. Type VII, as anchoring fibrils
questions.explanation: Type IV collagen forms the basal-lamina network (not fibrils); I is skin/bone/tendon, II cartilage, VII anchoring fibrils.

questions.question: Elastin provides:
questions.explanation: Elastin gives stretch and recoil (aorta ~50% elastin); interwoven collagen limits overstretch.

questions.question: Fibronectin functions to:
options: A. Seal the gaps at tight junctions
B. Resist compression as a hydrated gel
C. Form the axoneme of motile cilia
D. Attach the ECM to cells via integrins
questions.explanation: Fibronectin is a glycoprotein attaching ECM to cells; integrins link it to actin, and cell tension stretches it into fibrils.

questions.question: The enzymes that degrade the ECM for remodelling and migration are the:
questions.explanation: Proteases, especially MMPs, degrade ECM; activity is restrained by latent secretion, receptor confinement and inhibitors (TIMPs).

questions.question: The two main structural components of the basal lamina are:
options: B. Laminin and type IV collagen
questions.explanation: Laminin (organiser) and type IV collagen (network) build the basal lamina, with nidogen, fibronectin and perlecan.

questions.question: A filtering role of the basal lamina is seen in the:
questions.explanation: The glomerular basal lamina is a selective filter between blood and urine.

questions.question: From apical to basal, the epithelial junctions occur in the order:
options: C. Tight, adherens, desmosome, gap, then cell–matrix
questions.explanation: Apical→basal: tight junction, adherens junction, desmosome, gap junction, then cell–matrix (actin-linked and hemidesmosome).

questions.question: Cell–cell adhesion and cell–matrix adhesion are mediated, respectively, by:
questions.explanation: Cadherins mediate cell–cell adhesion; integrins mediate cell–matrix adhesion.

questions.question: Which junctions anchor to intermediate filaments?
options: A. Tight junctions and gap junctions
C. Adherens junctions and focal adhesions
questions.explanation: Desmosomes and hemidesmosomes link to intermediate filaments; adherens and actin-linked junctions bind actin.

questions.question: Cadherins bind with low affinity yet hold strongly because they:
options: A. Cluster, sharing load like Velcro
questions.explanation: Cadherins are homophilic and weak individually but cluster, sharing load (Velcro effect) while allowing remodelling.

questions.question: Tight-junction sealing strands are made of:
questions.explanation: Claudins and occludins form the sealing strands that force directional (transcellular) transport, e.g. gut glucose.

questions.question: A gap junction (connexon) allows passage of:
options: C. Ions and small molecules under ~1 kDa
questions.explanation: Connexons (6 connexins, ~1.4 nm pore) pass ions and small molecules (<~1 kDa), coupling cells electrically/metabolically, but not macromolecules.

questions.question: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by antibodies against which junction?
questions.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris = anti-desmoglein antibodies attacking desmosomes; bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomal proteins.

questions.question: Integrins bind ECM proteins via motifs such as:
questions.explanation: Integrins recognise ECM motifs like RGD outside and link via adaptors to the cytoskeleton (usually actin) inside.

questions.question: A hemidesmosome connects:
options: A. Two cells via gap-junction channels
B. The basal lamina to keratin intermediate filaments
C. Actin to the mitotic spindle
questions.explanation: Hemidesmosomes (integrin alpha6-beta4, collagen XVII, plectin) link the basal lamina to keratin intermediate filaments.

questions.question: 'Anoikis' is the death of a cell that:
options: A. Cannot form a gap junction
B. Loses integrin-mediated anchorage to the matrix
C. Fails to replicate its DNA
D. Runs out of GTP for microtubules
questions.explanation: Anoikis is apoptosis triggered by loss of integrin-mediated matrix anchorage (integrins signal survival, outside-in).

questions.question: Integrins signal in two directions; 'inside-out' signalling refers to:
options: A. The cell regulating its own grip on the matrix
B. Ions flowing through a channel
D. The matrix instructing cell survival
questions.explanation: Inside-out = the cell adjusts integrin grip; outside-in = matrix anchorage signals survival. Focal adhesions are mechanosensors.

musculoskeletal_system_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W1 PI · Musculoskeletal Introduction
musculoskeletal_system_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
musculoskeletal_system_mhhs2401.html.content: Skeleton = bones+cartilage+ligaments; 206 bones; functions: support, protection, mineral/lipid storage, blood cell production, leverage. Axial vs appendicular. Bone tissue: compact (osteons: central Haversian canal, lamellae, lacunae, canaliculi) vs spongy (trabeculae). Cells: osteoprogenitor, osteoblast, osteocyte, osteoclast. Ossification: endochondral (cartilage model) vs intramembranous. Growth at epiphyseal plate. Joints: functional (syn/amphi/diarthrosis), structural (fibrous/cartilaginous/synovial). Muscle: fascicle arrangements, pennate=force, parallel=range; compartment syndrome->fasciotomy. Upper limb nerves from brachial plexus; carpal tunnel=median nerve. Development from mesoderm. Achondroplasia=FGFR3 AD.

questions.question: The skeletal system is made up of:
questions.explanation: The skeletal system = bones + cartilage + ligaments (206 bones of varied shape and histology).

questions.question: How many bones are in the adult human skeleton?
questions.explanation: There are 206 bones: 80 axial (protection/core) + 126 appendicular (mobility/levers).

questions.question: How are the bones split between axial and appendicular skeletons?
questions.explanation: Axial = 80 (skull, vertebrae, ribs), appendicular = 126 (limbs + girdles).

questions.question: Which bone cell builds new bone matrix (osteoid)?
questions.explanation: Osteoblasts deposit osteoid (collagen I); once trapped they become osteocytes; osteoclasts resorb bone.

questions.question: Which bone cell resorbs (breaks down) bone?
questions.explanation: Osteoclasts resorb bone; the osteoblast-osteoclast balance sets total bone mass.

questions.question: The structural unit of compact bone is the:
questions.explanation: The osteon has a central (Haversian) canal, concentric lamellae, lacunae (osteocytes) and canaliculi.

questions.question: Growth in the LENGTH of a long bone occurs at the:
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal plate (hyaline cartilage) lengthens bone; when growth stops it becomes the epiphyseal line.

questions.question: The musculoskeletal system develops from which germ layer?
questions.explanation: MSK tissues arise from mesoderm; gastrulation forms the three germ layers.

questions.question: The shaft of a long bone is called the:
questions.explanation: Diaphysis = shaft; epiphysis = end; metaphysis = between them (holds the growth plate); medullary cavity holds marrow.

questions.question: A defining feature of a synovial joint is:
questions.explanation: Synovial joints have a cavity with hyaline articular cartilage, a capsule and synovial fluid (6 types).

questions.question: A mature bone cell sitting in a lacuna is a(n):
questions.explanation: Osteocytes are mature cells in lacunae; they sense mechanical load (Wolff's law) via canaliculi.

questions.question: Endochondral ossification forms bone by:
options: A. Depositing bone in a membrane
questions.explanation: Endochondral: mesenchyme to chondroblasts to a cartilage model that is replaced by bone (most long bones).

questions.question: Intramembranous ossification is characterised by:
options: A. A cartilage template forms first
B. Osteoblasts lay bone, no cartilage
D. Elongation at the growth plate
questions.explanation: Intramembranous: mesenchyme to osteoblasts laying osteoid directly - no cartilage model (e.g. flat skull bones).

questions.question: The periosteum has an outer and inner layer that are respectively:
questions.explanation: Outer fibrous + inner cellular (osteoprogenitor) layers; Sharpey's fibres anchor it; it is vascular and innervated.

questions.question: The FUNCTIONAL classification of joints is:
options: C. Hinge, pivot and saddle types
questions.explanation: Functional: synarthrosis (no movement), amphiarthrosis (slight), diarthrosis (free); structural is fibrous/cartilaginous/synovial.

questions.question: The STRUCTURAL classification of joints is:
questions.explanation: Structural: fibrous (suture, syndesmosis, gomphosis), cartilaginous (synchondrosis, symphysis), synovial (has a cavity).

questions.question: For a skeletal muscle, the origin and insertion are usually the:
options: A. The movable then the fixed end
D. The tendon and its own sheath
questions.explanation: Origin = fixed (usually proximal) attachment; insertion = movable (usually distal) attachment.

questions.question: A pennate fascicle arrangement trades:
options: A. More range for less force
B. More force for less range
questions.explanation: Pennate muscles pack many short fibres for more force but less range; parallel muscles give more range.

questions.question: In adults, red (blood-forming) marrow is found mainly in the:
options: A. The shafts of all long bones
C. The fingers and the toes
D. The cartilage of the joints
questions.explanation: Adult red marrow sits in axial bones and the proximal femur/humerus; a marrow biopsy is taken from the iliac crest.

questions.question: Wolff's law states that bone:
options: A. It never changes after growth
B. Built where loaded, lost if unused
C. It only grows during childhood
D. It dissolves under any stress
questions.explanation: Wolff's law: load builds bone (osteocytes sense strain) and disuse/bed rest loses it; trabeculae align to stress.

questions.question: In a somite, the myotome gives rise to:
questions.explanation: Somite derivatives: sclerotome to vertebrae/ribs, myotome to muscle, dermatome to dermis.

questions.question: The sclerotome of a somite develops into the:
questions.explanation: The sclerotome forms the axial skeleton (vertebrae and ribs).

questions.question: Achondroplasia is caused by a mutation in which gene?
questions.explanation: Achondroplasia is an autosomal-dominant FGFR3 mutation; thalidomide is the classic limb teratogen.

questions.question: Carpal tunnel syndrome is compression of which nerve, and where?
options: A. Ulnar nerve at the elbow
B. Median nerve under the flexor retinaculum
C. Radial nerve in the arm
D. Axillary nerve at the shoulder
questions.explanation: The median nerve is compressed under the flexor retinaculum (numb thumb-side fingers, weak grip).

questions.question: Compartment syndrome is treated surgically by:
questions.explanation: Bleeding/swelling in an inextensible fascial compartment chokes vessels/nerves; fasciotomy releases the pressure.

questions.question: A bone-marrow biopsy is most commonly taken from the:
questions.explanation: The iliac crest holds accessible adult red marrow and is the usual biopsy site.

questions.question: Outgrowth of the developing limb bud is driven by the:
options: C. The neural tube roof plate
questions.explanation: The AER at the limb tip drives proximodistal outgrowth; lateral plate mesoderm makes the skeleton, somites the muscle.

questions.question: Syndactyly (fused digits) results from failure of:
questions.explanation: Digits are freed by programmed cell death (apoptosis) between them; its failure leaves syndactyly.

questions.question: Bisphosphonate drugs treat bone loss by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclasts, slowing resorption to preserve bone mass (e.g. in osteoporosis).

questions.question: Which mesoderm gives rise to the limb SKELETON?
questions.explanation: Lateral plate mesoderm forms the limb skeleton; paraxial (somite) mesoderm supplies the limb muscle.

arm_elbow_forearm_mhhs2401_wk2.html.title: MHHS2401 W2 · Arm, Elbow & Anterior Forearm
arm_elbow_forearm_mhhs2401_wk2.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
arm_elbow_forearm_mhhs2401_wk2.html.content: Distal humerus: capitulum (lateral, radius head), trochlea (medial, ulnar trochlear notch); radial+coronoid fossae anterior, olecranon fossa posterior. Elbow = hinge; anular ligament at proximal radioulnar pivot joint. Epicondyle-olecranon triangle preserved in supracondylar fracture, lost in dislocation. Pulled elbow = anular ligament tear. Arm anterior (musculocutaneous: biceps, brachialis=pure flexor, coracobrachialis), posterior (radial: triceps). Pronation/supination = radius over ulna. Anterior forearm flexors median except FCU + medial half FDP (ulnar). Extrinsic hand muscles = remote control. Golfer's elbow = medial epicondylitis (flexor-pronator).

questions.question: The rounded lateral condyle of the distal humerus that articulates with the radial head is the:
questions.explanation: The capitulum (lateral, rounded) takes the radial head; the trochlea (medial pulley) takes the ulnar trochlear notch.

questions.question: What structural type of joint is the elbow?
questions.explanation: The elbow is a synovial hinge joint (capitulum-radius, trochlea-notch) allowing flexion/extension.

questions.question: Pronation and supination occur at which joints?
questions.explanation: The proximal and distal radioulnar (pivot) joints let the radius rotate over the ulna for pronation/supination.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies the anterior (flexor) compartment of the arm?
questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis); the radial nerve supplies the posterior.

questions.question: The chief extensor of the elbow is the:
questions.explanation: Triceps brachii (radial nerve) is the main elbow extensor; biceps and brachialis flex it.

questions.question: Besides flexing the elbow, biceps brachii is a powerful:
questions.explanation: Biceps is a strong supinator (most effective with the elbow flexed) as well as an elbow flexor.

questions.question: The radius and ulna are joined along their shafts by the:
questions.explanation: The interosseous membrane links radius and ulna and transfers load between them.

questions.question: The anterior compartment of the forearm mainly contains:
questions.explanation: The anterior forearm holds the flexors and pronators (+ extrinsic hand flexors); the posterior holds extensors.

questions.question: The common flexor origin of the forearm is the:
questions.explanation: The superficial flexors/pronators share a common origin on the medial epicondyle of the humerus.

questions.question: Medial epicondylitis is commonly known as:
questions.explanation: Medial epicondylitis (flexor-pronator overuse) is 'golfer's elbow'; lateral is 'tennis elbow'.

questions.question: Which part of the proximal ulna grips the trochlea of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The trochlear notch of the ulna (between olecranon and coronoid) grips the humeral trochlea.

questions.question: The anterior coronoid and radial fossae of the humerus receive, in flexion, the:
questions.explanation: In flexion the coronoid process and radial head swing into the anterior coronoid and radial fossae.

questions.question: The head of the radius is held against the ulna's radial notch by the:
questions.explanation: The anular ligament rings the radial head, holding it to the radial notch while it spins (pronation/supination).

questions.question: Which ligament reinforces the MEDIAL side of the elbow?
questions.explanation: The ulnar (medial) collateral ligament (three bands) reinforces the medial elbow; the radial collateral is lateral.

questions.question: The carrying angle of the elbow is:
questions.explanation: The carrying angle (arm-forearm axis) is typically greater in females and helps the swinging limb clear the hips.

questions.question: Which anterior arm muscle is a PURE elbow flexor, inserting on the ulna?
questions.explanation: Brachialis inserts on the ulna and is a pure flexor (its pull is unaffected by pronation/supination).

questions.question: Flexor digitorum superficialis lies in which layer of the anterior forearm?
questions.explanation: FDS is the single intermediate-layer muscle, between the superficial (4) and deep (3) anterior forearm muscles.

questions.question: The extrinsic hand muscles are described as a 'remote control' because they have:
options: A. Short bellies within the hand
B. Forearm bellies, long hand tendons
C. No tendons of any kind
questions.explanation: Their contractile bellies sit in the forearm while long tendons cross to the hand - power delivered at a distance.

questions.question: 'Pulled elbow' (radial head subluxation) is typical of:
options: B. Young children after a pull
questions.explanation: A sudden pull on a young child's arm tears/slips the anular ligament off the radial head (pulled elbow).

questions.question: In pronation and supination, which bone moves over the other?
options: A. The ulna over the radius
B. The radius over the fixed ulna
questions.explanation: The radius pivots over the relatively fixed ulna at both radioulnar joints, crossing over it in pronation.

questions.question: A fall on the hand with the elbow flexed classically causes:
questions.explanation: Force drives the distal humerus through the weaker anterior capsule, dislocating the elbow posteriorly.

questions.question: In elbow FLEXION, the two epicondyles and the olecranon form:
questions.explanation: In flexion they form a triangle; in extension they line up straight - a check used to detect dislocation.

questions.question: The long head of biceps brachii originates from the:
questions.explanation: Long head = supraglenoid tubercle (tendon over the humeral head); short head = coracoid; biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity.

questions.question: The long head of triceps brachii arises from the:
questions.explanation: The long head of triceps arises from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula.

questions.question: The proximal radius features a head, a neck, and a tuberosity that anchors the:
questions.explanation: The radial tuberosity is the insertion of the biceps brachii tendon.

questions.question: The distal radioulnar joint is a synovial pivot between the:
options: B. Ulnar head in the radius' notch
C. The radius and the carpus
questions.explanation: Distally, the ulnar head sits in the ulnar notch of the radius (a pivot), completing pronation/supination.

questions.question: Flexor pollicis longus (a deep anterior muscle) flexes which structure?
questions.explanation: FPL runs from the radius/interosseous membrane to the distal phalanx of the thumb, flexing it.

questions.question: Medial epicondylitis results from overuse of which muscle group?
questions.explanation: Repetitive wrist flexion + pronation microtraumatises the flexor-pronator common tendon at the medial epicondyle.

questions.question: 'Student's elbow' (olecranon bursitis) is inflammation of a bursa located:
questions.explanation: The subcutaneous olecranon bursa over the point of the elbow inflames with pressure/friction ('student's elbow').

questions.question: Pronator teres, part of the superficial anterior forearm, acts to:
questions.explanation: Pronator teres (medial epicondyle to mid-radius) pronates the forearm; it is a superficial flexor-compartment muscle.

bone_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W1 PIII · Bone Physiology I
bone_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
bone_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.content: Cells: osteoprogenitor->osteoblast (osteoid=collagen + hydroxyapatite)->osteocyte; osteoclast secretes acid (dissolves hydroxyapatite) + proteases. Osteocytes in lacunae connect via canaliculi/gap junctions. Compact: non-parallel collagen resists torsion; collagen+hydroxyapatite resists compression. Growth at epiphyseal plate until puberty. Remodelling: activation->resorption->reversal->formation. PTH & calcitriol raise blood Ca; calcitonin lowers. PTH continuous=catabolic, intermittent=anabolic (teriparatide). Vitamin D: skin/diet->liver(25-OH)->kidney(1,25 calcitriol). RANKL/OPG master switch. DEXA T-score<=-2.5 = osteoporosis. Osteogenesis imperfecta = collagen I defect.

questions.question: Which bone cell secretes bone matrix (osteoid)?
questions.explanation: Osteoblasts secrete osteoid (organic, mainly collagen I) that then mineralises with hydroxyapatite.

questions.question: Which bone cell resorbs bone?
questions.explanation: Osteoclasts secrete acid (HCl) and proteases to dissolve mineral and break down osteoid.

questions.question: A mature osteoblast trapped in the matrix becomes a(n):
questions.explanation: Osteocytes are former osteoblasts embedded in lacunae; they sense mechanical load.

questions.question: Osteoprogenitor cells are best described as:
options: B. Stem cells that form osteoblasts
questions.explanation: Osteoprogenitors are stem cells that differentiate into bone-forming osteoblasts.

questions.question: The main organic component of osteoid is:
questions.explanation: Osteoid is organic matrix (mainly collagen I); it then mineralises with hydroxyapatite (calcium phosphate).

questions.question: The structural unit of compact bone is the:
questions.explanation: Compact bone is built of osteons (concentric lamellae around a central canal); spongy bone is trabeculae.

questions.question: Longitudinal (length) growth of bone occurs at the:
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal (growth) plate between epiphysis and diaphysis lengthens bone until it fuses.

questions.question: Which hormone RAISES blood calcium?
questions.explanation: PTH raises blood calcium (chiefly by promoting resorption); calcitonin lowers it.

questions.question: Which hormone LOWERS blood calcium?
questions.explanation: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium; PTH and calcitriol (vitamin D) raise it.

questions.question: Osteocytes in their lacunae communicate with each other through:
questions.explanation: Canaliculi are tiny channels linking lacunae, letting osteocyte processes exchange nutrients and signals.

questions.question: Spongy-bone trabeculae are arranged so that they:
options: B. Align along lines of stress
questions.explanation: Trabeculae are not random - they align along stress lines (and remodel from microfractures), per Wolff's law.

questions.question: Osteoclasts dissolve the MINERAL of bone mainly by secreting:
questions.explanation: Osteoclasts pump out acid (HCl) to dissolve hydroxyapatite, while proteases break down the osteoid proteins.

questions.question: The active hormonal form of vitamin D is:
questions.explanation: Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol) is the active form; it raises calcium absorption.

questions.question: An increase in RANKL (with decreased OPG) drives:
questions.explanation: RANKL activates osteoclasts (resorption); OPG is a decoy that blocks it. Up RANKL/down OPG = resorption.

questions.question: Appositional growth (increase in bone diameter) occurs at the:
questions.explanation: Bone widens by appositional growth at the periosteum (osteoblasts add bone; osteoclasts widen the marrow cavity).

questions.question: Endochondral ossification forms bone by:
options: A. Depositing bone in a membrane
questions.explanation: Chondrocytes lay a cartilage foundation that osteoblasts then replace with bone (most long bones).

questions.question: In compact bone, non-parallel collagen fibres mainly provide:
options: D. The bone's main blood supply
questions.explanation: Interwoven (non-parallel) collagen resists twisting and gives tensile strength; mineral resists compression.

questions.question: Peak bone mass is typically reached by about what age?
questions.explanation: Peak bone mass (60-80% genetically determined) is reached by ~25-30, then gradually declines.

questions.question: How does the EFFECT of PTH depend on the pattern of exposure?
options: A. It always builds bone up
C. It always resorbs bone away
D. The pattern makes no difference
questions.explanation: Continuous PTH raises RANKL/lowers OPG (resorption); intermittent PTH is anabolic (used therapeutically).

questions.question: What is the correct activation pathway of vitamin D3?
options: A. Kidney to liver to skin
B. Skin to liver to kidney
questions.explanation: Cholecalciferol (skin UV/diet) is 25-hydroxylated in the liver, then 1-hydroxylated in the kidney to active calcitriol.

questions.question: OPG regulates bone by acting as:
options: B. A decoy receptor that blocks RANKL
questions.explanation: OPG is a soluble decoy for RANKL; more OPG (or less RANKL) shifts the balance toward bone formation.

questions.question: Osteoporosis is characterised by:
options: B. Excess osteoclast activity, bone loss
C. Too much collagen laid down
D. Always a single gene defect
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis is net bone loss (osteoclast hyperactivity / reduced endocrine suppression), giving fragile bone.

questions.question: Osteomalacia (rickets in children) is caused by:
questions.explanation: Osteomalacia/rickets is poor mineralisation of osteoid (commonly vitamin D deficiency), giving soft bones.

questions.question: Osteogenesis imperfecta results from:
options: B. A defect in collagen I
questions.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta ('brittle bone disease') is a collagen-I defect causing very fragile bones.

questions.question: Bone mineral density is measured clinically by:
questions.explanation: DEXA measures bone density; the T-score compares to young adults, the Z-score to same age/sex peers.

questions.question: In compact bone, blood reaches the osteocytes via the:
questions.explanation: Each osteon's central canal carries vessels; nutrients then diffuse via canaliculi to the osteocytes.

questions.question: Bone remodelling is described as 'coupled' because:
options: A. It only happens in children
B. Resorption is followed by formation
questions.explanation: Remodelling couples osteoclast resorption with subsequent osteoblast formation (activation-resorption-formation), lifelong.

pharmacology_intro_medi2004_wk1.html.title: MEDI2004 W1 · Introduction to Pharmacology
pharmacology_intro_medi2004_wk1.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
pharmacology_intro_medi2004_wk1.html.content: A drug = any substance producing a biological effect when administered. Drug (active chemical) vs medicine (formulated for therapy) vs drug class (grouped by action/target/use). Body-made substances (insulin) are drugs only when given externally. Pharmacology = study of drugs and their interactions with living systems; subdivisions: pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, pharmacotherapeutics, toxicology, pharmacogenetics, clinical pharmacology. PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body. Classes: analgesic, anaesthetic, anxiolytic, antihypertensive, antineoplastic, etc.

questions.question: A drug is best defined as:
options: A. Any substance that treats an infection
B. Any substance formulated as a tablet or injection
C. Any naturally occurring plant extract
D. Any substance that produces a biological effect in a living organism
questions.explanation: A drug is any substance that produces a biological effect when administered to a living organism — natural or synthetic, therapeutic or not.

questions.question: Which is NOT a recognised source of drugs?
options: B. Substances made only in a laboratory
questions.explanation: Drugs may be synthetic, natural (plants, animals, microorganisms) or products of genetic engineering — so 'lab-only' is false.

questions.question: Insulin made by the pancreas becomes a 'drug' when it is:
options: A. Administered to the body from outside
C. Broken down by the liver
D. Stored in the beta cells
questions.explanation: Substances the body makes itself (e.g. insulin) count as drugs only when administered from an external source.

questions.question: The difference between a 'drug' and a 'medicine' is that a medicine is:
options: A. A drug formulated for therapeutic use
C. A drug that occurs naturally
D. A drug with no side effects
questions.explanation: The drug is the active chemical; a medicine is that drug formulated for therapeutic use.

questions.question: A 'drug class' groups drugs that share a:
options: B. Mechanism, target or therapeutic use
questions.explanation: A drug class groups drugs by shared action, molecular target or therapeutic use.

questions.question: Pharmacology is the study of:
options: B. The manufacture of tablets and capsules
C. Drugs and their interactions with living systems
questions.explanation: Pharmacology is the study of drugs and how they interact with living systems.

questions.question: Pharmacology as a field has developed from:
options: A. Genetic engineering toward plant medicine
B. Synthetic chemistry back toward herbal remedies
C. Herbal and magical remedies toward evidence-based biopharmaceuticals
D. A purely theoretical to a purely herbal discipline
questions.explanation: The discipline has grown from herbal and magical remedies to modern evidence-based biopharmaceuticals.

questions.question: Which of these is a recognised subdivision of pharmacology?
questions.explanation: Subdivisions include pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, pharmacotherapeutics, toxicology, pharmacogenetics and clinical pharmacology.

questions.question: The branch of pharmacology concerned with the harmful effects of chemicals is:
questions.explanation: Toxicology studies the adverse/poisonous effects of drugs and chemicals.

questions.question: Pharmacokinetics describes:
options: A. How a drug is priced
B. What the body does to the drug
C. How a drug is discovered
D. What the drug does to the body
questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetics (PK) = what the body does to the drug (ADME); pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body.

questions.question: A drug's mechanism of action and its therapeutic effect are the domain of:
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamics (PD) covers the drug's mechanism and effect on the body; PK covers how the body handles it.

questions.question: The four processes summarised by ADME are:
questions.explanation: ADME = Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion — the stages of pharmacokinetics.

questions.question: Broadly, pharmacokinetics largely determines a drug's dose and timing, while pharmacodynamics determines its:
questions.explanation: PK sets dose/timing (how much drug is where, when); PD sets the effect and side effects.

questions.question: An analgesic is a drug class used to treat:
questions.explanation: Analgesics treat pain; anxiolytics treat anxiety; antihypertensives treat high blood pressure; antineoplastics treat cancer.

questions.question: An antineoplastic drug is used to treat:
questions.explanation: Antineoplastic = anticancer. Antidepressants treat depression, antipsychotics psychosis, antihypertensives high blood pressure.

questions.question: An anxiolytic is prescribed to:
questions.explanation: Anxiolytics reduce anxiety; sedatives calm/induce sleep; PrEP prevents HIV; analgesics relieve pain.

questions.question: PrEP belongs to a drug class used for:
questions.explanation: PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) is a drug class for HIV prevention.

questions.question: An antihypertensive is a drug class that:
questions.explanation: Antihypertensives lower blood pressure — the class name signals the therapeutic use.

questions.question: Which pairing of drug class and effect is correct?
questions.explanation: Stimulants increase alertness/activity; sedatives calm; analgesics relieve pain; anaesthetics produce loss of sensation.

questions.question: The subdivision that applies pharmacology to patient care and drug use in humans is:
questions.explanation: Clinical pharmacology applies pharmacological science to the safe, effective use of drugs in patients.

questions.question: Pharmacogenetics is concerned with how:
options: A. Drugs are absorbed across membranes
B. Genetic variation affects drug response
C. Drugs are grouped into classes
D. Drugs are excreted by the kidney
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenetics studies how inherited genetic differences influence a person's response to drugs.

questions.question: Which statement about drugs is correct?
options: A. A drug need not be therapeutic to count as a drug
B. A drug and a medicine are identical terms
C. Only externally sourced chemicals can have effects
D. Only synthetic substances are drugs
questions.explanation: A drug is anything producing a biological effect — therapeutic intent is not required; a medicine is the therapeutically formulated form.

questions.question: Pharmacotherapeutics is chiefly concerned with:
options: A. Using drugs to treat disease
B. The movement of drugs across membranes
C. Genetic variation in drug response
D. The toxic effects of drugs
questions.explanation: Pharmacotherapeutics is the use of drugs to prevent and treat disease.

questions.question: A hallucinogen is classed by its:
options: D. Ability to lower blood pressure
questions.explanation: Hallucinogens are grouped by their perception-altering action — a class defined by shared effect.

questions.question: Why is 'what the body does to the drug' the key idea of pharmacokinetics?
options: A. It describes the drug's receptor binding
B. It captures absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion
C. It sets the drug's chemical structure
D. It defines the drug's therapeutic class
questions.explanation: PK = the body's handling of the drug through ADME, which governs how much reaches the target and when.

questions.question: An anabolic steroid is classified primarily by its:
questions.explanation: Anabolic steroids are grouped by their tissue-building (anabolic) action.

questions.question: Which best captures the modern scope of pharmacology?
options: A. Only the herbal origins of remedies
B. Drugs and all their interactions with living systems
C. Only the beneficial effects of medicines
D. Only the manufacture of biologics
questions.explanation: Pharmacology spans all drug–living-system interactions, beneficial and harmful, natural and synthetic.

pharmacokinetics_medi2004.html.title: MEDI2004 W2 · Pharmacokinetics
pharmacokinetics_medi2004.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
pharmacokinetics_medi2004.html.content: PK = what body does to drug (ADME). Metabolism via cytochrome P450. Membrane crossing: passive (simple) diffusion dominates; active transport against gradient with energy. Absorption = site of administration -> plasma. pKa = pH at 50% ionised; ion trapping = only uncharged form crosses. Bioavailability F = fraction reaching systemic circulation; IV F=1.0, oral <1 (first-pass + incomplete absorption). Oral dose to match IV = IV/F. Sublingual/rectal partly bypass first-pass. PK params: AUC (exposure), Cmax, Tmax. Distribution: albumin binds acidic drugs, alpha1-acid glycoprotein binds basic; only free drug active. Vd = amount in body / plasma conc (apparent); low Vd stays in plasma (warfarin), high Vd = tissue/fat (paracetamol).

questions.question: Pharmacokinetics is 'what the body does to the drug'. Pharmacodynamics is:
options: A. What the drug does to the body
B. How the drug is discovered
C. How the drug is priced
D. How the drug is manufactured
questions.explanation: PK = the body's handling of the drug (ADME); PD = the drug's action and effect on the body.

questions.question: 'Pharmacokinetics' literally combines pharmaco (drug) with:
questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetics = pharmaco + kinetics: the movement/handling of the drug through the body.

questions.question: Which sequence lists the four stages of drug disposition in order?
questions.explanation: ADME: Absorption → Distribution → Metabolism (biotransformation) → Excretion.

questions.question: Which process moves a drug across a membrane WITHOUT using energy?
questions.explanation: Passive transport (paracellular, simple and facilitated diffusion) needs no energy; active transport and pinocytosis do.

questions.question: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in that it:
options: A. Moves against the concentration gradient
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion is passive (down the gradient, no energy) but needs a carrier; simple diffusion needs none.

questions.question: Active transport is distinguished by moving a drug:
options: A. Against its concentration gradient using energy
B. Down its gradient without energy
questions.explanation: Active transport uses carriers plus energy to move drug against the gradient.

questions.question: For most drugs, transmembrane movement is dominated by:
questions.explanation: Passive (simple) diffusion accounts for most drug movement across membranes.

questions.question: Absorption is the movement of a drug from:
options: A. The kidney into the urine
B. The site of administration into the plasma
C. The liver into the bile
D. The plasma into the tissues
questions.explanation: Absorption = entry from the administration site into the systemic circulation (plasma).

questions.question: Roughly how much of an oral drug is absorbed within 1–3 hours?
questions.explanation: Around 75% of an orally administered drug is typically absorbed within 1–3 hours.

questions.question: Which factor increases the rate of drug absorption?
options: D. Greater surface area at the absorbing site
questions.explanation: Absorption rises with surface area, lipid solubility and blood flow; it falls when these decrease.

questions.question: The pKa of a drug is the pH at which:
options: A. 50% of the drug is ionised
B. The drug is fully absorbed
D. The drug is completely un-ionised
questions.explanation: pKa = the pH at which a weak acid or base is 50% ionised.

questions.question: Which form of a weak-acid or weak-base drug crosses the lipid membrane?
options: A. Neither of the two forms
questions.explanation: Only the uncharged, lipid-soluble form crosses; the ionised form is water-soluble and does not.

questions.question: 'Ion trapping' occurs because the charged form of a drug:
options: A. Is inactivated by plasma enzymes
C. Is trapped where the local pH favours its ionisation
D. Freely crosses membranes in either direction
questions.explanation: Only the uncharged form crosses; once across, drug that ionises at the local pH is trapped (e.g. a weak acid trapped in plasma vs gastric juice).

questions.question: Which is an example of a parenteral (injection) route?
questions.explanation: Injection routes include SC, IM, IV, intra-arterial, intrathecal, intravitreal; sublingual/rectal/inhalation are non-injection.

questions.question: A drug placed under the tongue is given by the ___ route:
questions.explanation: Sublingual = under the tongue; it partly bypasses first-pass metabolism.

questions.question: On a concentration–time curve, Cmax represents the:
options: C. Total drug exposure over time
D. Time at which the peak occurs
questions.explanation: Cmax = peak concentration; AUC = total exposure; Tmax = time to peak.

questions.question: The AUC (area under the concentration–time curve) is a measure of:
questions.explanation: AUC quantifies overall drug exposure; Cmax is the peak and Tmax the time to it.

questions.question: Bioavailability (F) is the fraction of a dose that:
options: B. Reaches the systemic circulation unaltered
D. Is metabolised by the liver
questions.explanation: F = fraction of the administered dose reaching the systemic circulation in unchanged form.

questions.question: By definition, the bioavailability of an intravenous dose is:
questions.explanation: IV drug enters the circulation directly, so F = 1.0; oral F is usually lower.

questions.question: The main reason oral bioavailability is often below 1.0 is:
options: B. First-pass metabolism plus incomplete absorption
questions.explanation: Low oral F is mainly first-pass metabolism (gut wall/liver) combined with incomplete absorption.

questions.question: Which routes partly bypass first-pass hepatic metabolism?
questions.explanation: Sublingual and rectal routes drain partly to the systemic circulation, bypassing some first-pass metabolism.

questions.question: A drug has F = 0.5. To match a 50 mg IV dose, the oral dose should be:
questions.explanation: Oral dose = IV dose / F = 50 / 0.5 = 100 mg.

questions.question: If only 25% of an oral dose reaches the circulation, a 200 mg oral dose is equivalent to an IV dose of:
questions.explanation: Equivalent IV dose = oral dose × F = 200 × 0.25 = 50 mg.

questions.question: Which factor influences drug distribution?
options: A. The colour of the tablet
C. The brand of the drug
D. Blood flow to the tissue
questions.explanation: Distribution depends on tissue permeability, binding, pH partition, fat:water partition and blood flow.

questions.question: Body water makes up roughly what fraction of body weight?
questions.explanation: Total body water is about 50–70% of body weight, spread across plasma, interstitial, intracellular and transcellular compartments.

questions.question: Acidic drugs bind mainly to which plasma protein?
questions.explanation: Acidic drugs bind albumin; basic drugs bind alpha1-acid glycoprotein.

questions.question: Only which fraction of a drug in plasma is pharmacologically active?
questions.explanation: Only free, unbound drug can leave the plasma and act; bound drug is an inactive reservoir.

questions.question: Basic drugs bind preferentially to:
questions.explanation: Basic drugs bind alpha1-acid glycoprotein; acidic drugs bind albumin.

questions.question: Volume of distribution (Vd) is calculated as:
options: C. Amount of drug in the body ÷ plasma concentration
questions.explanation: Vd = total drug in body / plasma concentration — an apparent (not real) volume.

questions.question: A drug with a very LOW volume of distribution tends to:
options: A. Cross into all cells freely
D. Stay largely in the plasma
questions.explanation: Low Vd (e.g. warfarin ~0.14 L/kg) means the drug stays in plasma; high Vd means tissue/fat accumulation.

questions.question: Compared with warfarin (Vd ≈ 0.14 L/kg), paracetamol (Vd ≈ 1–1.2 L/kg):
options: A. Distributes more into tissues and body water
B. Is not distributed at all
D. Stays more confined to plasma
questions.explanation: A higher Vd indicates greater distribution out of plasma into tissue/body water.

questions.question: Vd is described as an 'apparent' volume because it:
options: A. Is measured directly by imaging
B. Equals total body water exactly
C. Need not correspond to any real physiological volume
D. Is the same for every drug
questions.explanation: Vd is a proportionality constant relating body drug to plasma concentration; it can exceed real body volumes and is not a literal compartment.

questions.question: The large non-polar compartment into which lipophilic drugs distribute is:
questions.explanation: Fat is the large non-polar reservoir; lipid-soluble drugs accumulate there (raising Vd).

questions.question: Which patient factor can alter drug absorption?
questions.explanation: Age, health status and genetic polymorphisms are patient factors affecting absorption.

questions.question: Why does the ionised fraction of a drug matter for absorption?
options: B. It cannot cross lipid membranes, limiting passive absorption
C. It is always more toxic
D. It is the only form that is active
questions.explanation: Ionised drug is water-soluble and cannot cross the lipid bilayer, so a higher ionised fraction reduces passive absorption.

respiratory_anatomy_pt2_mhhs2402.html.title: MHHS2402 W2 · Respiratory Anatomy II
respiratory_anatomy_pt2_mhhs2402.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
respiratory_anatomy_pt2_mhhs2402.html.content: Neck posterior triangle: CN XI, brachial plexus, subclavian vessels. Carotid sheath: vagus (X), internal jugular vein, common carotid. Larynx cartilages: thyroid, cricoid (only complete ring), arytenoid, corniculate, epiglottis; true cord=vocal fold. Posterior cricoarytenoid = only abductor; recurrent laryngeal supplies all intrinsic except cricothyroid. Ribs: true 1-7, false 8-10, floating 11-12. Diaphragm hiatuses: caval T8, oesophageal T10, aortic T12; phrenic C3-5 -> referred shoulder pain. Intercostal bundle VAN in costal groove; chest drain above the lower rib. Parietal pleura=somatic (pain), visceral=autonomic. Right lung 3 lobes (oblique+horizontal), left 2 lobes+cardiac notch. Type I pneumocyte=gas exchange, Type II=surfactant.

questions.question: Which laryngeal cartilage is the only COMPLETE ring?
questions.explanation: The cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring; the thyroid is a shield and the arytenoids are paired.

questions.question: The 'true' vocal cords are also known as the:
questions.explanation: The true cords are the vocal folds (phonation); the false cords are the vestibular folds.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) provides motor and sensory supply to the diaphragm ('C3,4,5 keep the diaphragm alive').

questions.question: How many lobes does the LEFT lung have?
questions.explanation: The left lung has 2 lobes (oblique fissure) plus a cardiac notch; the right has 3.

questions.question: How many lobes does the RIGHT lung have?
questions.explanation: The right lung has 3 lobes (oblique + horizontal fissures); the left has 2.

questions.question: Which alveolar cell produces surfactant?
questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes make surfactant; Type I pneumocytes are the thin gas-exchange cells.

questions.question: Gas exchange across the alveolar wall occurs mainly through which cell?
questions.explanation: Thin Type I pneumocytes form most of the alveolar surface for gas exchange; Type II make surfactant.

questions.question: The main muscle of quiet inspiration is the:
questions.explanation: The diaphragm increases the vertical dimension of the thorax in quiet inhalation; external intercostals assist.

questions.question: Which pleura directly covers the lung surface?
questions.explanation: Visceral pleura covers the lung; parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the posterior boundary of the anterior triangle / anterior boundary of the posterior triangle?
questions.explanation: Sternocleidomastoid (SCM) divides the neck; trapezius forms the posterior border of the posterior triangle.

questions.question: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is the ONLY abductor of the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor (opens the cords); the others adduct or tense them.

questions.question: Most intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (from the vagus) supplies all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid.

questions.question: The suprahyoid muscles act to:
questions.explanation: Suprahyoids (e.g. digastric, mylohyoid) elevate the hyoid/larynx; infrahyoids depress them.

questions.question: Which pleura is pain-sensitive, and why?
questions.explanation: Parietal pleura has somatic innervation (intercostal + phrenic) and is pain-sensitive; visceral pleura is not.

questions.question: True ribs (1-7) attach to the sternum by:
questions.explanation: True ribs each have their own costal cartilage to the sternum; false ribs (8-10) share, and 11-12 float.

questions.question: The central non-muscular part of the diaphragm is the:
questions.explanation: Muscle fibres converge on the central tendon; the crura anchor it to the lumbar vertebrae.

questions.question: The oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm is at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: Oesophageal hiatus = T10 (with the vagus); caval hiatus = T8; aortic hiatus = T12.

questions.question: In the costal groove, the intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in what order (top to bottom)?
questions.explanation: From superior to inferior it is Vein, Artery, Nerve (VAN) - guiding safe needle placement below a rib.

questions.question: The cardiac notch is a feature of which lung?
questions.explanation: The cardiac notch (and lingula) is on the left lung, making room for the heart.

questions.question: Phonation (voice production) occurs at which laryngeal division?
questions.explanation: The glottis (the vocal folds + rima glottidis) is the phonation region; supraglottis protects the airway.

questions.question: The caval opening (IVC) passes through the diaphragm at which level?
questions.explanation: The caval hiatus is at T8, through the central tendon (with the right phrenic nerve).

questions.question: The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm lies at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus is at T12 (behind the diaphragm, transmitting aorta, thoracic duct, azygos).

questions.question: The internal laryngeal nerve provides which function?
options: B. Sensation above the vocal cords
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal (branch of superior laryngeal) is sensory to the supraglottic mucosa; the external supplies cricothyroid (motor).

questions.question: The external laryngeal nerve supplies which single muscle?
questions.explanation: The external laryngeal nerve is motor to cricothyroid (which tenses the cords); the rest go to the recurrent laryngeal.

questions.question: How do the bronchial arteries differ from the pulmonary circulation?
options: A. They carry blood for gas exchange
B. They nourish lung tissue (from aorta)
C. They drain the heart chambers
D. They form part of the airway
questions.explanation: Bronchial arteries (from the thoracic aorta) nourish the lung tissue; the pulmonary circulation does gas exchange.

questions.question: Why is the RIGHT main bronchus the more common site of foreign-body aspiration?
options: A. It is longer and much narrower
B. It is wider, shorter, more vertical
C. It has no cartilage rings
D. It lies further to the left
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled objects tend to lodge there.

questions.question: The conducting zone of the airway differs from the respiratory zone in that it:
options: B. Has no alveoli and no gas exchange
D. Is only in the nose
questions.explanation: The conducting zone (trachea to terminal bronchioles) moves air but has no alveoli/gas exchange; the respiratory zone does.

questions.question: The right oblique fissure of the lung roughly follows which rib?
questions.explanation: The oblique fissure runs from about T4 along the 6th rib to the 6th costochondral junction.

questions.question: Phrenic nerve palsy typically causes:
options: C. Loss of rib movement only
questions.explanation: Losing phrenic supply paralyses a hemidiaphragm, which then sits raised (and moves paradoxically).

questions.question: In the pulmonary plexus, sympathetic activity to the airway causes:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic (SNS) activity dilates the bronchi (bronchodilation); parasympathetic (vagus) constricts them.

cell_organisation_study_guide.html.title: MEDI2200 W1 · Cell Organisation
cell_organisation_study_guide.html.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
cell_organisation_study_guide.html.content: Plasma membrane = fluid mosaic: phospholipid bilayer (heads out, tails in) + proteins. Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus + organelles; prokaryotes do not. Nucleus: double membrane + pores, chromatin, nucleolus (makes ribosomes). Rough ER (ribosomes) = protein synthesis; smooth ER = lipids/steroids + detox. Golgi modifies/sorts/ships (cis receives from ER -> trans ships). Lysosome = acidic (~4.5-5) digestion, autophagy; peroxisome = oxidation, catalase breaks H2O2. Mitochondrion = double membrane, cristae, makes ATP. Cytoskeleton: microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments, microtubules (tracks + spindle). Centrosome = MTOC + centrioles, builds spindle. Ribosomes = protein synthesis.

questions.question: The plasma membrane is best described as a:
options: A. Double layer of DNA and RNA
C. Rigid single layer of protein
D. Fluid mosaic of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins
questions.explanation: The membrane is a fluid mosaic: a phospholipid bilayer studded with proteins.

questions.question: In the phospholipid bilayer, the fatty-acid tails are arranged:
options: D. Facing inward, away from water
questions.explanation: Hydrophilic heads face the watery surfaces; hydrophobic tails point inward, away from water.

questions.question: Integral (transmembrane) proteins are held in the bilayer by:
options: A. Covalent bonds to the phosphate heads
D. Hydrophobic regions interacting with the lipid tails
questions.explanation: Integral proteins have hydrophobic segments that sit among the lipid tails, anchoring them in the bilayer.

questions.question: Which feature defines a eukaryotic cell but is absent in prokaryotes?
questions.explanation: Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles; prokaryotes lack both.

questions.question: Compared with eukaryotes, prokaryotic cells characteristically:
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles.

questions.question: The nuclear envelope is a double membrane perforated by:
questions.explanation: The double-membraned nuclear envelope is studded with nuclear pores that control traffic.

questions.question: The nucleolus, inside the nucleus, is the site of:
questions.explanation: The nucleolus transcribes rRNA and assembles ribosome subunits.

questions.question: The DNA–protein complex housed inside the nucleus is called:
questions.explanation: The nucleus contains chromatin (DNA plus packaging proteins), the nucleolus and nucleoplasm.

questions.question: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is studded with which structures?
questions.explanation: Rough ER carries ribosomes on its surface and synthesises proteins.

questions.question: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum specialises in:
options: C. Lipid and steroid synthesis and detoxification
questions.explanation: Smooth ER makes lipids and steroids and carries out detoxification; rough ER makes proteins.

questions.question: Which organelle modifies, sorts and packages proteins for shipping?
questions.explanation: The Golgi modifies, sorts and ships proteins and lipids.

questions.question: Proteins arriving at the Golgi from the ER enter at which face?
questions.explanation: The cis face receives cargo from the ER; the trans face ships it out.

questions.question: Lysosomes contain which kind of enzymes?
questions.explanation: Lysosomes hold acid hydrolases for digestion and autophagy.

questions.question: Lysosomal digestive enzymes are most active at a pH of about:
questions.explanation: The lysosome interior is kept acidic (~4.5–5), the optimum for its hydrolases.

questions.question: Which organelle uses catalase to break down hydrogen peroxide?
questions.explanation: Peroxisomes carry out oxidation reactions and use catalase to detoxify H2O2.

questions.question: A key difference between a peroxisome and a lysosome is that the peroxisome:
options: B. Carries out oxidation rather than acidic digestion
C. Produces most of the cell's ATP
D. Is filled with acid hydrolases
questions.explanation: Peroxisomes oxidise substrates (catalase handling H2O2); lysosomes do acidic hydrolytic digestion.

questions.question: Which organelle is the main site of ATP production?
questions.explanation: The mitochondrion generates most of the cell's ATP.

questions.question: The cristae (folds) of the inner mitochondrial membrane serve to:
options: D. Maximise surface area for ATP production
questions.explanation: Cristae increase the inner-membrane surface area for the ATP-generating machinery.

questions.question: Uniquely among most organelles, mitochondria contain their own:
questions.explanation: Mitochondria have their own DNA (and a double membrane), reflecting their endosymbiotic origin.

questions.question: What is the function of ribosomes?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes translate mRNA into protein.

questions.question: Ribosomes bound to the rough ER predominantly make proteins destined for:
questions.explanation: ER-bound ribosomes make secreted, membrane and organelle-targeted proteins; free ribosomes make cytosolic proteins.

questions.question: Which cytoskeletal element forms the mitotic spindle and acts as transport tracks?
questions.explanation: Microtubules build the spindle and act as tracks; actin drives movement, intermediate filaments give strength.

questions.question: Cilia and flagella are motile structures built from:
questions.explanation: Cilia and flagella are built from microtubules (the 9+2 axoneme) driven by dynein.

questions.question: The centrosome, with its pair of centrioles, acts as the cell's:
questions.explanation: The centrosome (MTOC) nucleates microtubules and builds the mitotic spindle.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the secretory (export) pathway?
options: A. Nucleus → Golgi → rough ER → membrane
B. Rough ER → Golgi → vesicle → plasma membrane
C. Golgi → rough ER → vesicle → plasma membrane
D. Rough ER → lysosome → Golgi → membrane
questions.explanation: Proteins are made in the rough ER, modified/sorted in the Golgi, then shipped in vesicles to the membrane.

questions.question: Ribosomal RNA is transcribed and ribosome subunits assembled in the:
questions.explanation: rRNA is transcribed and ribosome subunits assembled in the nucleolus.

questions.question: A primary role of the plasma membrane is to:
options: B. Control what enters and leaves the cell
questions.explanation: The selectively permeable membrane regulates exchange between the cell and its surroundings.

questions.question: The self-digestion of worn-out organelles is carried out by the:
questions.explanation: Lysosomes perform autophagy — digesting the cell's own worn-out components.

questions.question: The mitochondrion is bounded by:
questions.explanation: Mitochondria have two membranes; the inner one folds into cristae.

questions.question: Why must a secreted protein pass through both the ER and the Golgi?
options: A. The ER destroys it and the Golgi rebuilds it
B. Both organelles independently synthesise the protein
C. Made in the ER, then processed in the Golgi
D. The Golgi makes it and the ER exports it
questions.explanation: Rough ER synthesises the protein; the Golgi then modifies, sorts and packages it for export.

respiratory_anatomy_pt1.html.title: MHHS2402 W1 · Respiratory Anatomy I
respiratory_anatomy_pt1.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
respiratory_anatomy_pt1.html.content: Skull: 22 bones (8 cranial + 14 facial); key respiratory bones = ethmoid & sphenoid. Ethmoid: cribriform plate (roof), perpendicular plate (septum), conchae (lateral wall). Nasal septum = perpendicular plate of ethmoid + vomer + septal cartilage. Cranial fossae: anterior (frontal/ethmoid/sphenoid), middle (sphenoid/temporal), posterior (temporal/occipital). Foramen=through, fossa=sit in, sinus=air cavity. CN I olfactory through cribriform plate; CN V trigeminal (face sensation + chewing) V1 superior orbital fissure, V2 foramen rotundum, V3 foramen ovale (all sphenoid); CN IX & X through jugular foramen (posterior fossa). Olfactory nerve != bulb != tract.

questions.question: Which two skull bones are the key 'respiratory' bones of the nasal airway?
questions.explanation: The ethmoid (roof/walls/upper septum) and the vomer (lower septum) build the bony nasal airway.

questions.question: The lower bony nasal septum is formed by which bone?
questions.explanation: The bony septum = perpendicular plate of the ethmoid (above) + the vomer (below).

questions.question: Which cranial fossa is the most anterior?
questions.explanation: The anterior cranial fossa is most forward; its floor includes the cribriform plate of the ethmoid.

questions.question: The olfactory nerve (CN I) reaches the brain by passing through the:
questions.explanation: Olfactory axons pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid to the olfactory bulb.

questions.question: The chief role of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) is:
options: D. Taste at the back of the tongue
questions.explanation: CN V is the main sensory nerve of the face (with motor fibres to the muscles of mastication).

questions.question: In bone terminology, a 'foramen' is:
options: B. A hole or opening in bone
questions.explanation: A foramen is a hole/opening in bone through which nerves or vessels pass.

questions.question: The glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves leave the skull through the:
questions.explanation: CN IX, X and XI exit via the jugular foramen; CN I uses the cribriform plate and CN V the sphenoid foramina.

questions.question: Which cranial nerve carries the sense of smell?
questions.explanation: The olfactory nerve (CN I) carries smell from the olfactory epithelium through the cribriform plate.

questions.question: The ethmoid contributes ALL of the following to the nasal cavity EXCEPT the:
questions.explanation: The ethmoid gives the cribriform plate, perpendicular plate and superior/middle conchae; the vomer is a separate bone.

questions.question: The cribriform plate forms part of the floor of which fossa?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate floors part of the anterior cranial fossa (and roofs the nasal cavity).

questions.question: The three divisions of the trigeminal nerve all exit through foramina in which bone?
questions.explanation: V1 (superior orbital fissure), V2 (foramen rotundum) and V3 (foramen ovale) all pass through the sphenoid.

questions.question: Which trigeminal division exits through the foramen rotundum?
questions.explanation: V2 (maxillary) exits via foramen rotundum; V1 via the superior orbital fissure; V3 via foramen ovale.

questions.question: The superior and middle nasal conchae are projections of which bone?
questions.explanation: The superior and middle conchae are ethmoid; the inferior concha is a separate bone.

questions.question: The respiratory mucosa lining the nasal cavity chiefly serves to:
options: B. Warm, humidify and filter air
questions.explanation: Respiratory mucosa warms, humidifies and filters inspired air before the lower airway.

questions.question: Olfactory receptor neurons are located in the:
options: A. The floor of the mouth
questions.explanation: The olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity holds the smell receptors.

questions.question: The crista galli, an attachment for the falx cerebri, is a projection of the:
questions.explanation: The crista galli projects up from the ethmoid's cribriform plate.

questions.question: The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms which part of the septum?
questions.explanation: The perpendicular plate forms the upper bony septum; the vomer forms the lower, and cartilage the front.

questions.question: The ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal exits the skull through the:
questions.explanation: V1 leaves via the superior orbital fissure; V2 the foramen rotundum; V3 the foramen ovale.

questions.question: The mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal exits through the:
questions.explanation: V3 exits via the foramen ovale (and is the only trigeminal division carrying motor fibres).

questions.question: Besides IX and X, which other cranial nerve passes through the jugular foramen?
questions.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI (glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory).

questions.question: After crossing the cribriform plate, olfactory axons synapse in the:
questions.explanation: Olfactory nerve fibres synapse in the olfactory bulb, which projects via the olfactory tract to the brain.

questions.question: The middle cranial fossa is largely formed by which bone and houses which lobes?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid (with the temporal bone) forms the middle fossa, which cradles the temporal lobes.

questions.question: The nasal conchae improve air conditioning mainly by:
options: D. Storing a reserve of air
questions.explanation: The scroll-like conchae increase mucosal surface area and create turbulence, warming/humidifying/filtering air.

questions.question: Which single bone provides the cribriform plate, crista galli, perpendicular plate and two conchae?
questions.explanation: All four are parts of the ethmoid - the central bone of the nasal airway.

posterior_forearm_wrist_mhhs2401_wk3.htm.title: MHHS2401 W3 PI · Posterior Forearm & Wrist
posterior_forearm_wrist_mhhs2401_wk3.htm.subject: Musculoskeletal System
posterior_forearm_wrist_mhhs2401_wk3.htm.content: L4: posterior forearm extensors, hand bones, wrist joint, fractures and healing.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies every muscle of the posterior forearm compartment?
questions.explanation: All posterior-compartment muscles are supplied by the radial nerve or its deep branch (posterior interosseous nerve); a proximal lesion causes wrist-drop.

questions.question: Which posterior-compartment muscle is the exception that flexes the elbow and never crosses the wrist?
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis lies in the extensor compartment but its tendon passes anterior to the elbow axis, so it flexes the forearm and inserts on the distal radius without crossing the wrist.

questions.question: Extensor carpi ulnaris acting with flexor carpi ulnaris produces which movement?
questions.explanation: Pairing an extensor and flexor on the same (ulnar) side cancels their flex/extend actions and adds their side pull, giving ulnar deviation.

questions.question: The central (medial) band of the extensor expansion inserts on which structure?
options: A. The base of the distal phalanx
B. The base of the middle phalanx
questions.explanation: The central band inserts on the middle phalanx (extends the PIP joint); the two lateral bands rejoin on the distal phalanx (extend the DIP joint).

questions.question: After piercing the supinator, the deep branch of the radial nerve continues as which nerve?
questions.explanation: The deep branch passes between the two heads of supinator (through the arcade of Frohse) and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve to the deep extensors.

questions.question: Biceps brachii is the more effective supinator when the elbow is in which position?
questions.explanation: Biceps supinates powerfully with the elbow flexed (e.g. driving a screw); the supinator muscle dominates when the elbow is extended or for slow, unresisted turning.

questions.question: Which tendons form the medial and lateral borders of the anatomical snuffbox?
options: A. Medial: EPB + APL; lateral: EPL
B. Medial: EPL; lateral: EPB + APL
questions.explanation: Extensor pollicis longus (which hooks Lister's tubercle) forms the medial border; extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus form the lateral border.

questions.question: Lateral epicondylitis is chiefly a microtrauma of the common origin of which muscle?
options: D. The supinator in the fossa
questions.explanation: Overuse strains the common extensor origin, especially extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB); pain is over the lateral epicondyle and worsens on resisted wrist extension.

questions.question: Radial deviation of the wrist is limited to roughly 15 degrees by which structure?
questions.explanation: The radial styloid projects further distally than the ulnar styloid and abuts the carpus, capping radial deviation at ~15 degrees (ulnar deviation is freer).

questions.question: How many carpal bones are there in each wrist?
questions.explanation: Eight carpals sit in two rows of four: proximal (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform) and distal (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate).

questions.question: Which three parts make up a metacarpal (and each phalanx)?
questions.explanation: Each long bone of the hand has a proximal base, a shaft (body) and a distal head; a boxer's fracture breaks the neck/shaft of the 5th metacarpal.

questions.question: What is the proximal carpal row, from lateral (radial) to medial (ulnar)?
questions.explanation: Proximal row lateral to medial: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Mnemonic: Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle.

questions.question: Why does a scaphoid waist fracture risk avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment?
options: A. It is the largest carpal with the thinnest cortex
B. Its blood supply enters distally and runs retrograde
